page_title: How to Implement a Search Engine Part 1: Create Index

summary.title: How to Implement a Search Engine Part 1: Create Index
summary.one_liner: You learn how to build an inverted index with positional postings over a Wikipedia article collection in Python, including tokenizing, stop-word filtering, Porter stemming, and saving the index to a text file.
keywords: how does a search engine index documents
takeaways: An inverted index maps each term to a postings list of documents, and for phrase queries each posting also stores term positions.
Parsing steps: concatenate title and text, lowercase, tokenize on [a-z0-9], remove stop words, then stem with Porter Stemmer.
Build a per-page index and merge it into the main in-memory dictionary, appending postings for each term.
The index is saved as text lines in the form term|docID:pos,pos;docID:pos, so a separate query program can read it.
Stemming made indexing about five times slower in the author's tests, and term frequencies roughly follow Zipf's Law.
summary.summary: The article is the first part of a series building a search engine over roughly 40,000 to 50,000 Wikipedia articles, using a prebuilt XML-like file. It explains the corpus structure and the three query types it will support: one-word, free text, and phrase queries. It then walks through the parsing pipeline and builds a worked example of a positional inverted index on three small documents, showing how per-page indexes are merged into the main dictionary. The post also defines the text file format used to save the index and reports timing, size, and term statistics for a 5,000-document test collection and a full collection. The code is in Python, and the author links a downloadable workspace.
